title: Report leaves family of student killed by Winnipeg police with 'more unanswered questions'
subtitle: Afolabi Stephen Opaso, 19, was shot dead during well-being check on Dec. 31, 2023
article: The family of Afolabi Stephen Opaso, a Nigerian international student who was shot and killed by a Winnipeg police officer nearly two years ago, is calling for a new investigation into his death after a watchdog report written last week by Alberta authorities found "no reasonable grounds" to charge the officer with a criminal offence.

Opaso, 19, was studying at the University of Manitoba when died in hospital on Dec. 31, 2023, after police shot him in a University-Crescent apartment during a well-being check for mental health concerns.

A written decision by the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team 's director Matthew Block, published on Aug. 27, says it was "necessary" and "reasonable" for the officer to use his firearm because Opaso was armed with two knives.

ASIRT took over the investigation in January 2024 after Manitoba's Independent Investigations Unit flagged a "potential conflict" because a Manitoba Justice employee was a "close relative" of the involved officer.
For two years, the family has been asking for answers. On Friday, Afolabi's sister, Yemisi Opaso, said the report answered very few.
"The whole family, we are really disappointed ... we are now in more pain because we have so many unanswered questions," Yemisi Opaso said during a voice call at a Friday news conference.
"Instead of clarity, we are now left with more, more, more questions, more unanswered questions," she said.
One of the family's lawyers, Jean-René Dominique Kwilu, said the family wants a new investigation, claiming ASIRT's probe was an "utter disgrace" that was marred by bias.

"It seems as though the blue wall is protecting another blue wall," Kwilu said, questioning ASIRT's impartiality when former police officers worked on the investigation. "The family thinks they are trying to cover their tracks, to put a narrative together."
Benjamin Nkana Bassi, who is also a member of the family's legal team, said one of the key issues in the report is whether Opaso ran at the officers, according to the witness officer's claims.
According to the report, "there is also no evidence that contradicts [Witness Officer1's] evidence that [Opaso] came at them with knives."
Bassi argues that there was no evidence that confirms Opaso ran at them, noting civilian witnesses did not report hearing running in the apartment during the incident.
"If Mr. Afolabi Opaso did not run, it means there was no threat, it means they killed him for nothing," Bassi said. "This is what led the family to believe that this is fabricated evidence."
"This is a joke of a report. It's not independent, it's not impartial. It's simply a disgrace," Kwilu said.
The family's lawyers said they will be writing to Prime Minister Mark Carney and Premier Wab Kinew, as well as the federal and provincial attorneys general.

Kwilu said the family wants to see city officials, including the mayor and chair of the police board, start requiring officers to wear body cameras. The family is calling on the province to expand mental health supports, including adding more mental health staff to help police respond to well-being calls.
The province included funding for 25 mental health workers to work alongside law enforcement in its 2024 budget.
"The fight will continue. If they thought that somehow this report would make [the family] go quiet, they're sadly mistaken," Kwilu said.
CBC News has reached out to ASIRT but did not immediately hear back.
